utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to greet everyone present, Prosecution, counsel, and the accused. We'll be continuing with our work. We will be calling a witness into the courtroom, but first I have two oral decisions that I would like to render and also a request the Chamber would like to make. As far as the oral decisions are concerned, the decision regarding the admission into evidence of documents concerning witness Senada Basic. The Chamber shall hereby state its position with regard to the admissibility of documents that relate to witness Senada Basic who was heard on the 25th of October, 2006. The Chamber shall admit into evidence the following documents presented by the Prosecution, since they have a certain probative and certain relevance: P 09711, P 07350. In addition, the Chamber notes that the Defence hasn't requested any documents to be admitted into evidence. Second decision concerns admission into evidence of documents relating to Witness BW. The Chamber will hereby render a decision with regard to the admission into evidence of documents relating to the witness BW who was heard on the 19th October 2006. The Chamber will admit into evidence the following documents presented by the Prosecution as they have certain probative value and certain relevance: IC 00058 under seal, IC 00059 under seal, IC 00060 under seal, P 01326, P 09152, P 09151, P 09153, P 09154, P 09155, P 09163. The Chamber will also admit the following documents presented by the Defence given that they have certain probative value and certain relevance: 3D 00472 under seal, P 01472 under seal, 3D 00454. And now I will slowly read out the following decision, and I would like the Prosecution to listen carefully, as well as the Defence, but the Prosecution is particularly concerned by this: The title of the decision is invitation of the parties to forward to the Chamber -- to submit to the Chamber their arguments on the admission of documents into evidence. The Chamber would like to draw the parties' attention to an important procedural issue that concerns admission -- the admission of documents into evidence. The Chamber would first of all like to point out that pursuant to the decision on admission into evidence of documents rendered on the 13th of July, 2006, a party that wishes to tender a document into evidence should do so in principle through a witness who is in a position to testify with regard to document's reliability, relevance, and probative value. The document that is being tendered into evidence must be shown to a witness called into the courtroom. According to this same decision, the Chamber allows for an exception to this principle. The Prosecution may file a written motion with the Chamber requesting that documents that haven't been shown to a witness be admitted into evidence provided that a certain number of strict conditions have been met. These conditions are governed by guideline number 6 of this decision. One of these conditions is the condition according to which these written motions must be filed within an eight-day time limit or eight days subsequent to the appearance of a witness who could have testified with regard to the documents the Prosecution would -- is tendering into evidence. As a result, the admission into evidence of a document via written submission means that the Chamber must have heard a witness who testified with regard to the circumstances that the document in question relates to. Pursuant -- as part of the application of the 13th of July decision, the Chamber would like to point out a number issues. First of all, among the documents mentioned in the 65 ter list provided by the Prosecution, there are also documents that are important and that could clarify certain matters for the Chamber with regard to the chain of command and with regard to the military structure of the HVO. The Chamber also notes that on a number of occasions the Prosecution attempted to present such documents through so-called crime base witnesses, witnesses who were not the most appropriate ones to testify with regard to these documents. In addition, the Chamber notes that the Prosecution has never filed any written motions pursuant to guideline number 6. As a result, the Chamber would like to know whether in the interest of justice and truth it might not be appropriate to modify somewhat the conditions mentioned in guideline number 6. This could be done by allowing the Prosecution to file, within certain limits, written motions requesting the documents that do not relate to the testimony of witnesses be admitted. The Chamber would like to point out that it is not its intention to substantially depart from the 13th of July, 2006, decision. The Chamber still subscribes to the basic principle governing the admission into evidence through witnesses. This principle was mentioned in the decision of the 13th of July. The Chamber nevertheless would like to amend the current procedure in order to sure that documents which are necessary for the case are tendered and admitted into evidence. The Chamber therefore invites the parties to submit their submissions, either written or oral submissions, by the 6th of November, 2006, at the latest. The Chamber would like to insist on the fact that the parties have already been heard with regard to the applicable law relating to the admissibility of documents into evidence, and this is not an issue that will be debated again. The Chamber would only like to hear the position of both parties with regard to the form and conditions that have to be met by a written motion requesting that certain documents that were not presented in the proceedings be admitted into evidence. And finally, the Chamber draws the attention -- draws the attention of the Prosecution to the fact that the Prosecution must select documents that are strictly necessary to determine matters in dispute. As a result, it is not possible to tender into evidence all documents referred to in the 65 ter list. So this is the invitation the Chamber is making to the parties. We would like to hear what your positions are by the 6th of November, 2006. Very briefly, the purpose of this decision is as follows: There are certain documents, for the moment the documents are Prosecution documents but the time will come when the Defence will be in an identical situation. There are documents that can be not be shown to a witness because the witness is not here or cannot come, et cetera, et cetera, but it's in the interest of justice for these documents to be admitted. As a result, a party can submit or could submit a written motion requesting that these documents be admitted into evidence in spite of the fact that this is not being done through a witness. To be quite clear, since if one wants to be clear it's best to put things clearly, this now concerns HVO documents or documents that concern the HVO. We've used up about a quarter of our time for these proceedings so far, but not single member of the HVO military has appeared here. As a result, the Prosecution when they want to present documents from the HVO presented documents to witnesses who were not in a position to recognise these documents. The situation might be similar for the Defence. If the Defence wants to have ABiH documents presented but they haven't got any witnesses from the ABiH at their disposal, they will be in a similar situation. So we have a perfect balance between the parties, and this would be in the interest of justice. So please give some thought to the matter by the 6th of November at the latest. Inform us of your positions. Naturally, you should read the transcript very carefully again since everything has been stated there. Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is an issue that has been heard in open session and in private sessions, too, recently, and it could have certain consequences, negative consequences. It concerns the general security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We referred to this when we were trying to decide whether certain witnesses should be granted protective measures. I believe that the decisions have been quite cavalier sometimes. I believe that the general security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not such that one should feel unsafe. In the last ten years much progress has been made in this area. There are courts in -- that have been integrated between Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are state institutions. Staff has been trained in accordance with the highest criteria and in accordance with UN bodies. The legal system has also been amended under the auspices of the UN and under the IPTF. Today in Bosnia-Herzegovina there are security and intelligence agencies that have been functioning for a while, and police bodies, throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ministry of Defence for Bosnia and Herzegovina has been established. There is no reason to say that there are no institutions that can guarantee security. In 2001, I backed a study for the World Bank on obstacles to investment in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time the security situation wasn't mentioned as an obstacle for foreign investment. I believe that we have good reason to believe that the security situation is satisfactory. I don't want to say that there are no problems, that there have been no terrorist acts, but property has been returned to everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to all those who fled. It's possible to speak freely in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to journalists, investigations as far as the freedom of press is concerned, it's in the 18th position in the world. So Bosnia and Herzegovina isn't the Wild West. And if we're discussing these matters here, perhaps the media isn't covering this to a great extent, but somebody is taking note and those who wonder whether to invest in Bosnia-Herzegovina will be informed of these notes. If there is no foreign investment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it can't survive economically. This is why I think that the issue of general security should be set aside and one shouldn't send negative messages from here to those who might want to help Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your comments on security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Perhaps the Prosecution will respond a little later, because I believe, Mr. Scott, that you would like to request protective measures for a witness. Yes, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be taking the witness today, and indeed there is an application for protective measures. Would Your Honour like me to address that application now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll move into private session, and we'll lower the blinds so that we can call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the needs of the proceeding will you give me your first and last name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Muamer Trkic. I was born on the 22nd of August, 1977, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told me a moment ago, but for the record what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work with metal. I am a welder by occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before in an international or national court of justice about the facts that occurred that your country at the time when you were 16 or is this, for you, the first time in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the first time for me to testify in court. I have never done it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question: You were heard in your country by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor. Were you also interrogated by an investigator of your own country within the framework of any proceedings conducted in your country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no. I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will you please read the text that is going to be given to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. I am going to give you some information, though I assume that the Prosecutor has already told you about this during your meeting yesterday or this morning. You will be asked to answer questions that will be put to you by Madam Gillett, who is going to have questions for you, and you will have to answer those questions, and you will see a screen in front of you with the text in English. So there is no point in looking at the screen if you don't understand English. On the other hand, if you do, you can refer to the screen. Once this has been completed, the Prosecution has envisaged an hour and a half, they may reduce this time. The Defence counsel, who are numerous, but there's only one for each accused, will be asking you questions as part of the cross-examination to -- this is to check the reliability of what you have said or perhaps to ask you some questions that are of particular interest to them in view of the facts alleged in the indictment. We are usually four Judges, but in application of 15 bis, we are three today. The three Judges in front of you may at any point in time ask you questions. As a rule, if the parties ask you the questions that we had in mind, we don't need to ask you anything in addition to that, but we might intervene to specify a particular point. Should you have any kind of difficulty, please let us know. If everything passes well, your testimony will be completed today, which means you will be able to return home tomorrow at the latest. We have some time left up until the break, so, Madam Gillett, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, you understand what His Honour the Judge said. You will be testifying in open, public session. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, if you could start off by answering these questions that I'll put to you. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf, the village of Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where have you lived for most of your life?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I spent most of my life in Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, just to give the Court an idea of where this village of Zdrimci is, how far away is Zdrimci from the town of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Three kilometres between the place where I live, but up to the end of the village it's four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what's the name of the nearest village to Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The name of the village is Vrse. That is the closest village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how far away -- how far away is the village of Vrse from the village of Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a kilometre, maybe a kilometre and a half on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, to the best of your knowledge is your village, the village of Zdrimci, the only village you know by that name in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's the only village known by that name. I don't know of any other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Before the war can you describe the ethnic composition of the village of Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand your question. The word "ethnic," could you explain that for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dealing with the period before 1993, what groups of people lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you mean by "groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What nations or nationalities. "Nations" would be the most appropriate terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand better if we use the terminology of "nationality"? What nationalities were living in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Muslims lived in the area I lived in, but the majority were Croats. And when the war started, that is January, when the conflict break out, then the Croats came, that is the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, before we get into any further detail about what happened during the war, are you able to say how many -- you say the Croats were in the majority in your village. Are you able to say how many more Croats than Muslims there were in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I think there were two and a half times more Croats than Muslims in Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did the Muslims and the Croats all live in the same part of the village, or were they in different parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: At the entrance to the village are only Croats. To the left there are a few Muslim houses but also some Croats, and then about a hundred metres later Muslims again, and after that it's all Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were these different areas that you've just described, did they all fall under the name of the village of Zdrimci, or were there different names given to these areas?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: All of this is the village of Zdrimci, but there are various names given to each part. Each part of the village has its name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And can you help us with what those names were?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As you enter the village there's a settlement inhabited by Croats, and it is known as Perici. To the left there's a location called Polici in which there may be 10 Muslim houses but there are also Croat houses. And then straight on from Perici you come to Trkici. That is where I live. Those are Muslims. And then when you pass Trkici, you have an area inhabited by Croats mostly bearing the surname of Sekerija.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, before the war what was the relationship like between the Muslims and Croats living in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I had cases when relations were super. They couldn't be better. That is how those relations were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did this relationship change at some point?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several days before, maybe four or five days before, I went to buy something in a shop in Perici. I was going to buy a drink, some drinks, but they refused. They said there were no drinks for balijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you say several days before, when was this? What period of time are we talking? The year and the month and the exact date if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I said this was before the 18th of January. Shall we say four or five days before the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mention shooting started. On what date was this?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The 18th of January, at 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where were you when the shooting started on the 18th of January?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I was in Munib Trkic's house. They had a basement. That is where the women were. And above the basement there was a business area, and that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And why were you in Munib Trkic's house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I and my father and another five or six men from the neighbourhood were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there any reason that you were in Munib Trkic's house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The reason was that soldiers could be seen coming from outside. There are hills outside the village, and we could notice soldiers. So I suppose we expected something to happen, and that is why we went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you mention these soldiers, do you recall what these soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They were wearing camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you notice any badges or any insignia on the camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Not straight away because there was a certain distance, but later on when I was captured I did notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Before we get to your capture, when you're describing what happened on the 18th of January you describe shooting at 6.00 in the morning. Which direction was the shooting coming from?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There's a small hill called Baba. I think it is to the south-west of the village, and that is from where the shooting mostly came.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you able to tell what kind of shots were being fired, what was being used to fire the shots?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what kind of weapons they were, as I was a minor, but I heard from the people who were with me that these were 120-millimetre mortars and anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you see what was being shot at?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I saw that they were falling mostly on the village, on the houses. That is where the shells mostly fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you see any damage as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The shells were falling and they hit houses, and several houses fell down. They mostly fell on the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long did this shooting last?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, about two hours, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where were you throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I was there in Munib Trkic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where about in Munib Trkic's house were you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I was above the basement, the floor above the basement, which was used for business premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you remember how many people were with you in -- on the floor above the basement?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There were about six to eight men as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any shots fired back in response to this shooting?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: In response to the shooting there was no response because there were only a couple of rifles. And while the shooting lasted, the people who had houses close to Croat houses at a distance of some 50 metres, they did respond, because during the shooting automatic rifles were fired from Croat houses and set fire to barns. So maybe some ten bullets were fired to allow them to release the cattle from the barns.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was that successful? Were the cattle released from the barns?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were those three barns on fire there, and they let all the livestock out of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the shooting lasted for about two hours. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, after the shooting you could hear a megaphone. They spoke through a megaphone. They said everyone should go out. Everyone should the basement and should surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you or anyone else in the house do as they were asking? Did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't leave immediately. We were afraid. We thought they might start shooting again, so we didn't leave immediately. And then they told us to leave. They said this through the megaphone again. They said we should surrender and said that they would start shooting again if we didn't surrender.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. The interpreters are asking if you could raise your voice a little bit. Perhaps sit a little closer to the microphone so they can pick up what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you were saying that through the megaphone you were asked again if you would surrender. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, no one went out again. As I have said, everyone was afraid. No one had much experience. We all thought they would start shelling again, so no one went out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And so what did they do when you refused to surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, they started shelling again, just as they had done the morning. At 6.00 in the morning, they continued shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: At any point on that day did you come to leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, no one left the house. Perhaps after an hour or so had passed the shooting stopped, and we saw that there were, well, perhaps about ten soldiers advancing. They had a Muslim man that they were escorting. I knew him. So they approached. They came very close. No one opened fire on them. They stood behind a house. They came close to us, and they said if no one left the basement they would use a Zolja to fire on the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you say that you know this Muslim man that was with the group of 10. Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: His surname is Catic. There are two brothers. One is called Kemo and the other Hilmo. He was one of the two brothers. I can't remember what his name was exactly, or I can't remember which one, but his surname was Catic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have just said that they threatened to use a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher. What is a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a sort of weapon. I'm really not very familiar with these weapons. I was quite young. I think it's used to fire a sort of rocket. It's some sort of hand-held launcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned with this person whom you've identified as Catic were 10 soldiers. Which army were those soldiers from?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers were from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you remember what those soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were wearing camouflage uniforms, and they had some sort of a sticker or badge on their shoulder on which it said "HVO."

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did they have -- sorry. Did this group come into the house where you were?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We immediately started leaving the basement. We all went out to the road by the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you remember how many there were in total? You mentioned before there were around six or eight men with you on the ground floor. Do you remember how many other people were there?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There were perhaps, as far as I can remember, 10 HVO soldiers there, and then other HVO soldiers arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people came out of the house that you had been in?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: About six men, six or seven men went out, and there were about 10 women there, too. They also went out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, once you were all outside the house, what happened to you all then?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: They told us that no one should try to flee. If we did, they said they would kill everyone. They said we should walk in front of them, and we should tell them where there were other people -- where the other people were, in which basements they were staying, and they wanted them to come out too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did they succeed in getting those people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in response to a question put to you by the Prosecution when asked whether there was any reaction, whether anyone fired back when the houses were shelled, you said that there was no reaction from your shelter but that there was certainly some reaction from certain Croatian houses, if I have understood you correctly, and now we realise that HVO soldiers entered the village and tried to get you to come out. My question is as follows: The people who were in the houses from which fire was opened in response to the attack, were these people Muslims or Croats, and did they also come out with you in the presence of HVO soldiers? The people who returned fire after having been attacked by the HVO, did they also come out with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. We all came out, and we all gathered at this one location with the women. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you haven't answered the question precisely. It's very important for us. Were there TO members or ABiH members in your village who protected you and who were armed, who protected you against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were only people from the surrounding villages, from the neighbourhood. My uncle and father were there, such people. They had a couple of rifles, and they returned fire from the houses that were close to the barns that were on fire. And they were the same location that I was at. And when they came to get us out of the basement, they were there as well, and they were disarmed and they also came out and went to the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we are. That's a question one should have put to you from the outset. So you are telling us that there were men in your village who had rifles, and they returned fire. They opened fire on the HVO. And when the HVO entered the village, the HVO disarmed them. That's what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did your father have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. He had a rifle. An M-48 rifle, that's what he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did he buy this M-48? Was it given to him? How did he get this rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He bought that rifle with his own money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But why did your father buy a rifle? Was it to hunt birds or rabbits? Why did he have an M-48?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said at the beginning, you could feel the presence of troops for a few days, so he bought this rifle and some other people -- several other people from the neighbourhood also bought rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many rifles were there in total, if you know? If you don't, just say that you don't know. How many rifles were there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were between three or four rifles, approximately. Where I was at least. As far as other places are concern, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you under the impression that there was a leader? Was anyone in command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. There were no commanders. They were all ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that people were gathered and brought out of the houses. Once this occurred, did you all remain together in one big group?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: We were in a group when we went out. When we went to the next basement, they also came out of the next basement. They asked them to come out of the second basement, and the third and the fourth basement, as far as I know. And then we were all assembled in the village and -- and the men were then separated from the women.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And having been through this process and been to -- I think you mention at least four basements, do you remember how many people were in that group when you were gathered, having been to those four basements?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I know that there were about 35 men, perhaps 40. I don't know exactly, but there were about 30 or 35 men. I really don't know how many women there were though.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether there were more women than men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were more women than men.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you said that the men were separated. Were you in that group of men that were separated off from the women?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there with the men.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened to you and the other men at that point?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There were HVO soldiers in front of us and behind us, and they said that we should set off in a certain direction. There was a garage that we arrived at, and they placed us in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I believe you mentioned Sekerija. Whereabouts was Sekerija?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: When you pass through these Muslim houses that I lived in, 300 metres later, you have an area that is called Sekerija. It's called Sekerija because there are Croats who have that surname who live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this garage that you arrived at, do you recall how big the garage was?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was four metres wide and 12 metres long as far as I can remember, roughly speaking. I don't know how large it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was on the floor of the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There was nothing, just concrete. There was a concrete floor, and the ceiling was made of concrete too. There were some planks that had been put together, so when they locked us in, we put these planks on the ground and sat down on these planks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you were locked in. How were you locked into the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: They closed the door, locked it and, naturally, put a chain on the door as well and locked it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you say "they," how many people is "they," and who were these people?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them there were exactly, but they were all HVO soldiers. They were strangers. I had never seen any of them before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: After the chain was put on the door to lock you in, did any of those HVO people stay at the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Two guards stayed there. I knew one of them. His name was Luka. I knew the other one, too, but I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, amongst those of you who were detained in the garage, how -- how old were the people in the garage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Ms. Gillett. He has just said that he knew one of the two guards. His name was Luka. I believe that you should put a question to the witness about this. Luka, was this an HVO soldier that you knew because he lived in that village? How is it you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yell, when the troops dispersed while we were locked in, I heard certain voices as they were dispersing, and then these two guards appeared, and I knew this person. His name was Luka. He was a Croat from the village there. And I knew the other one, too, but I didn't know his name. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this person called Luka, had you seen him in the village before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. He'd spent his entire life in Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while he was guarding you, was he wearing camouflage uniform? Did he have a weapon, and did he have a badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he didn't have a uniform on him. He was slightly elderly man. He had a rifle. I don't know what kind of a rifle he had, but he wasn't in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. He was wearing civilian clothes, but he had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your opinion, what was he doing with the HVO since he was in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know. They had probably left him there and assigned him the task of guarding us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges want to know whether Luka was a member of the HVO. You tell -- you've told us that he was wearing civilian clothes, and you said that perhaps the HVO had asked him to guard you. Does that mean that the HVO had asked a Croat from the village to guard you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't have an HVO badge, or he wasn't in uniform, but they probably told him that he was to stand guard. He must have received some sort of an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, among the HVO soldiers in the village -- well, were all the HVO soldiers in the village in camouflage uniforms and did they have badges, or were there members of the group who obeyed orders, who worked with all the others but who weren't in uniform, as was the case with Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of them were in uniform, but Luka, he was a somewhat elderly man, and the man he was with was also elderly. I don't know his name. They didn't have uniforms of any kind. They were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were members of the group, and they worked with other HVO members without any problems then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how this worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please move on, Ms. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, regarding the people in the garage with you, the men in the garage with you, were they civilian or military men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Most of them were soldiers. There were perhaps about 10 men who were over 60 years of age. I was the youngest one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you say that most were soldiers. Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, none of them were wearing uniforms. They should probably all have bought a uniform, but they can't have had the money so they were all in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And to which army did they belong?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know which army they belonged to. I really don't know that. They were probably members of the ABiH, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said that most of them were over 60 years of age and that you were the youngest. Those who were between 17 and 60, where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were there where I was too. They were held in the same garage that I was held in. They were there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, if you could just clarify. Approximately how many of the men were over the age of 60 that were in the garage with you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there were more than 10 men who were over 60 years of age, but I really can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the conditions in the garage, you mentioned that you were locked into the garage. What would happen if you wanted to go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, when we had to go to the toilet, when we asked to go to the toilet, they wouldn't open up. We had a pail, a bucket in the corner, and they said that we should use that to relieve ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: When we were locked in after night had fallen, they brought a bucket of milk, a canister of milk, several kilos of bread, and there were a few tins. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned after night had fallen this happened, and you spend the night in that garage.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all spent the night in that garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what about the next day? What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, we were there locked up. No one came.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long in total did you spend in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: About 11 days in total. I think these others -- the other people spent some more time there, but I don't know how long exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How, were you in that garage for the entire 11 days, or were there any occasions on which you left the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. After two days they said we should go to the neighbouring village of Vrse to tell them what had happened to us so that they would surrender too. So two days later, I went out. I also went to see my mother. She wouldn't allow me to go to Vrse, so then I returned to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, when you say that they said that you should go to the village of Vrse, who was saying this to you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know this person. He was a stranger.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was he a civilian person or a military person?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: A military person.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: From which military?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: A member of the HVO military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have the break now since it's a quarter to 4.00. We'll resume in 20 minutes' time, at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Gillett, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, just before the break you were describing how you had been asked to go to Vrse, and you'd said that there was a member of the HVO military who had asked you to do this. Was it just you who was asked, or were other people asked to go to Vrse?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My cousin was with me, Mirsad. His name was Mirsad. He's two years older than me, and so the two of us were told to go there to tell them this at Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you said that you went to see your mother and that she didn't want you to go to Vrse. How long did you stay with your mother?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I spent the night there with my mother, and the next day we returned to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where was your mother?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: They were in houses. They didn't chase them away or force them to go anywhere. They just told them to stay in the houses, but there were soldiers patrolling everywhere so that they stayed in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, once again, the soldiers that you mention patrolling everywhere, which soldiers were these?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: HVO. They belonged to the HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you recall how many soldiers there were patrolling?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. There were groups passing by, groups of three that would be on patrol, but I don't know exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you say you spent the night with your mother, and then you'd mentioned previously, prior to the break, that you returned to the garage. When you returned to the garage, were you asked any questions by the guards at the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. These were different people now, so they didn't know. Probably they hadn't discussed it amongst themselves, the guards, so they just shut us up again because we were young. So they didn't ask us anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You say these were different people. Do you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know those men.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How many men were they?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: There were again two.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, was there any other occasion on which you came to leave the garage during those 11 days that you spent there?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two days later, as far as I can remember, maybe three, HVO soldiers came to the door and asked who would volunteer to bury two bodies. One body was in the middle of the village. It was the body of Ihdija Trkic, and the other body was in Ahmo Catic -- in the house, and it was Ahmo Catic's body.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You say the HVO soldiers came to the door and asked who would volunteer. Who did volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I volunteered and a man called Catic. I think his name was Kemal. And another man, but I can't remember his name or who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you've described roughly where these two bodies were in the village itself. Did you see the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because we first went to collect the body of Ihdija Trkic. It was on the road in the middle of the village. We put him in a wheelbarrow and we drove him to the cemetery, and then we went back to fetch the other body, of Ahmo Catic, and we put him in the wheelbarrow, too, and took him to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Dealing first with the body of Ihdija Trkic. What condition was the body in when you found it?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The body was -- there was just one wound. I didn't see the rest of the body, but there was a bullet wound on his forehead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what about the other body, that of Ahmo Catic? What condition was that body in when you came to it?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: We found him on his bed. This was an older man of some 70 years old, I think, and he had seven or eight bullet wounds on his chest, stomach, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know how either of these two men came to die?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I heard when we were burying them under guards, there were guards there, soldiers, HVO soldiers were guarding us while we were digging the graves, and I heard from them that Ahmo Catic had been killed when they entered the house. They heard the man coughing, and they fired through the door and that is how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you had finished digging the graves, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: We were taken again to the garage where the others were locked in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, once again, after your return to the garage, was there any other occasion on which you had cause to leave the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I had one other occasion when they asked me, and I must underline I was the youngest. They asked me to bring a sheep from the village, so I left the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where did you go to when you left the garage on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I went to find the sheep, and as I was passing through the village where the civilians were, the Muslims, I saw a gathering of women there standing in front of the mekteb, and I heard an HVO soldier asking them to repeat after him the prayers, and he was crossing himself, and he said they all had to repeat after him and who failed to do so he would kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you hear what he was asking them to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was showing them how to cross themselves with his hand. And I can't remember exactly the words he used, but it was a prayer to God. And then there was another group standing there who were cursing Allah and everything Muslim, and they said that they would set fire to the mekteb, which was right there in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: This other group that was standing there cursing, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Also HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that they said they would set fire to the mekteb. At this time, what condition was the mekteb in?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: It was in a normal condition. It was an older building and there were a couple of bullet holes on the front, but otherwise it was in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see this mekteb again after this day?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed with my mother again on that occasion, and I -- I didn't see it being torched, but I saw it again when it had burnt down. A day or two later, I saw that the mekteb had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know who was responsible for it burning down?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Probably when the HVO soldiers said that they would set fire to it, probably they did it, though I didn't see who actually set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, on this third occasion you were away from the garage, did you later, after you'd moved the sheep, did you return to the garage again?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't return to the garage again. I stayed with my mother nonstop. So I was seen by HVO soldiers, but I was young and they didn't require me to go back to the garage again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And whereabouts was your mother?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: She was in the house next to mine. It was our neighbour's house, Husein Trkic's house, which was next door to mine, and she was there together with two or three other women. And these other women were in other houses, two or three to each house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving back briefly to your time in the garage, those 11 days that you've mentioned, how were you treated whilst you were detained in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I personally was treated well, but others, for example Salko Brica, he was beaten regularly if he were to ask something. He couldn't speak too well. He couldn't pronounce the words, and then he would be beaten most.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for beating him?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Marko Vukadin would come by. He was from the village from our neighbourhood. I knew him. He was the only one I knew. I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was Marko in the military?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He also wore a camouflage uniform, and he belonged to the HVO army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Apart from Salko Brica that you mentioned, do you know of any others who were beaten from the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They also beat Vahid Sakic. They beat him up, too, but not as much as Salko Brica. They took Dzulejman Memic out, and Halil Brica. They would take them out to dig their own graves, and when they did, they would force them to lie down and then cover them up with earth except for the face, and then they would fire a couple of bullets close to their heads, forcing them in that way to give them the information they wanted to hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, apart from Marko Vukadin whom you've mentioned, was there anybody else who was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: In the garage where the men were, I didn't know any others. They were all strangers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier the number of people that were in the garage with you, somewhere between 35 and 40. Did that number stay the same throughout your time in the garage, or at some point did anybody leave or did others join you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No other people came to join us, but people did leave. They took away between 10 and 15 men. I don't know exactly. They put them on a bus, and they took them away. I heard later that they were taken to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I wonder if you could take a look at Exhibit 1413. I believe it might be by the side of you there on the ELMO. If you'd turn to the B/C/S version under tab 1413, and you'll see a list of names there. If you'd turn to the second page of that list, you will see starting at number 49 there are names, and next to those names written the name Zdrimci. Were any of those people with you in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: People from number 49 up to 56 were taken away. From 49 to 57. They were no longer in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know anything about those listed in numbers -- from numbers 58 to 61?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: The names that are listed from number 58 to number 61 on that same document, were those people, people in the garage with you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These men, these others were in the garage. They stayed behind. These were also taken to Prozor. I heard later that they were taken to do forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, at the time you were in the garage those listed from numbers 58 to 61, were they still in the garage with you or did they go to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I know from -- for the names from 49 to 57, that they went to Prozor. As for these others, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you could turn now to the next tab, which is Exhibit 1636 in that same bundle of documents in front of you. And once again you'll see that there's a list. If you look at the B/C/S version, turn over the two English pages and to the B/C/S version. Again, on that first page, if you look down to number 26 and 27, you'll see that the village of Zdrimci is mentioned next to two names. Again, were those two persons listed, either of them, in the garage with you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were with me in the garage, from -- number 24, he was taken away. 25, he was also taken to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And numbers 26 and 27, did they remain in the garage or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I think they left, but I'm not sure. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you'd just turn over to the next page you'll see that the list continues, and more towards the bottom of the list, from number 24 of that list, again you see the village of Zdrimci, down to number 34. Were any of these people with you in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The name under 26 I think remained in the garage. Asim Trkic. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you'd turn over the page, there should be another list. And over one more from that, yes. If you take a look at that list, from numbers 24 to 34, again the village of Zdrimci is mentioned and there are names next to the village of Zdrimci. Were any of those people in the garage with you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The name under 24 was, so was number 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, up to number 34. Yes, they were with me in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you know if any of these people left the garage to go to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. Number 24 left. Number 26 also left, and number 25, 27 also, 28, 29, 30. As for the others, I'm afraid I am not quite sure whether they left or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, we've talked a little bit about -- you've explained what happened to you and others who were in the garage. You'd mentioned that you went away from the garage following moving some sheep and that you stayed with your mother. Now, what condition was your mother in and, indeed, the other women in that house when you reached her?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I saw that my mother's hands had burns, as well as my sister's. Their hands were covered with burns, and when I asked them what had happened, they said that when HVO soldiers came to torch houses with petrol they would pour the petrol on the houses, and then they, the women, would go out to try and put out the fires with their hands, and that's how they got their burns.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the situation that you've been describing in your village, in Zdrimci, how long did the situation remain as you've been describing?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The situation was like that until the first conflict stopped, that is, until there was a kind of -- of truce. But when that was exactly, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximate idea of when that might have been, whether it was a matter of days, weeks, or months?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really can't be precise about it. Was it 40 days or a month or 40 days, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned you were staying with your mother still in Zdrimci. Did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I was with my mother for as long as this situation lasted, until the truce. And when things calmed down, I went to my mother's -- my sister's, together with my mother and the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where was that, your sister's?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: In Vrse, about a kilometre or a kilometre and a half from Zdrimci. That is where my sister had got married, and we went to stay with her.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why did you not go back to your own house in Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: We were afraid of a repetition, because it still wasn't too safe. We stayed with my sisters. And then there's a small hill and we could see the village from it, and we watched a house being set on fire. So we didn't dare go down again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know at that time anybody by the name of Zanfula?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a woman from the village. She was Munib Trkic's sister and she lived across the road from us. She got married to someone from Bugojno, and when the conflict started she happened to be there. So, yes, I knew her.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with her once the conflict had started?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any contact with her. I had no problems with her, but I heard from other women that she was with the HVO, and she would tell them if they wanted to beat up someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what nationality was she?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: She was Muslim by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mention that you stayed with your sister in Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When did you return to Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I returned in 2003 when the house was rebuilt, and that is when I started living there again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: After the shooting that you describe that took place on the 18th of January, what conditions were the houses and buildings in Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Some were hit by shells. Some were burnt down. They weren't all burnt straight away, and they weren't all hit. Some were, some were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were these all the houses, both Muslim and Croat?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, only Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which documents would you like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: The two exhibits that I presented to the witness bearing Exhibit numbers 1413 and 1636.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You planned for an hour and 30 minutes. The Defence has an hour and 30 minutes, which means 15 minutes for each Defence team unless you divide this up amongst yourselves. Who will be starting?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will, but first of all, could the usher help me provide the Chamber with some of the documents that I have prepared for the cross-examination. There's only one document that I have in the file.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day. I have a few questions I with like to put to you. Could you tell me what happened on that day that you have been discussing, the day on which HVO soldiers arrived at the house that you were in. Was your father in that house at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was your father taken to the garage together with you and the other men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. In the meantime, I didn't even see him at the time. I only saw that he had disappeared later on, but how this happened I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "in the meantime"? When was the last time that you saw you father?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I saw my father when we call went out. He was there too. We were all there. When we set off it the other basement, well, that's when I no longer saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were there any other men who appeared in this way and then disappeared? Did you notice that any other men had left?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. They were all there, but I didn't notice when my father disappear.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So would it be correct to conclude that during that 40-day period, that's the time that you spent there, during that period you didn't see your father?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, no. I didn't see him until some sort of a truce had been established. I only heard that he had been killed. When someone asked about him, they'd say he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you met him in Vrse, in the village of Vrse, when your entire family met in your sister's house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned the death of two individuals, Ihdija Trkic and Ahmo Catic. You told us how Ahmo Catic was killed. You heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you go to search for his body when you were assigned to do this digging? Did you go to search for his body?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It was brought somewhere close to the positions where you were digging.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand. Which body are you referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking about Ahmo Catic. You said he was killed in his house. Did you go to his house on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where did you find him when you arrived in the house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: He was on the bed that he slept in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was that in the bedroom?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the bedroom. On the bed that he slept on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did you hear about Ihdija Trkic? Did you hear about how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: While they were taking us to the garage, you could hear some shooting, and I heard that he had opened fire on HVO soldiers, and on that occasion they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Was there both a mekteb and a mejtef in your village? I know that you know what we are talking about. Can we say -- can you describe what a mekteb and a mejtef is?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: A mekteb and mejtef, it's the same sort of thing. It's a mosque without a minaret. If it doesn't have a minaret, then it's a mekteb or a mejtef.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you believe that it's the same thing. It's not quite identical, but in your village there was a mosque without a minaret, and that was the mekteb.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in your statement -- in the course of your testimony today you said when you arrived there and when you saw an HVO soldier praying, you said that the mekteb hadn't been burnt down on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, it hadn't been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And after that point in time when did you notice that the mekteb had been burnt down? Did you notice that while you were still in the village of Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several days later, I don't know exactly how many days later, I noticed that it had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You saw that it had been burnt down, but you didn't see anyone setting fire to it. You don't know who the perpetrator of this act was?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that after all these events you did not stay on in the village of Zdrimci because you were afraid that a conflict might break out again? Is that why you left your house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge asked you whether you had already given any statements to any investigative bodies in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You said that you hadn't or you couldn't remember; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: However, I would like to remind you of something. Perhaps you have forgotten this, but it is important for certain reasons for me to show a document to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOVICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the following document on e-court 2D 00205. And I would also like to ask the usher for assistance. Could the usher show this statement to the witness so that he can have a look at a hard copy of the statement so that he can have a look at his signature to see whether it's his signature and to see whether he remembers this statement. It's not in the e-court system. I think it was provided on Friday. But in that case, we'll place it on the ELMO. Could we just have a look at the bottom of the statement so that we can see the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have a look there. Is this your signature? Have a look at the document to your right -- to the right. You see where the usher is, where the young lady is. Can you see your signature on the document? Do you remember having given this statement?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I didn't understand your question. The question was whether I had given any statements -- if the question had been whether I had given a statement to the police, then I would have remembered having given that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at the first page. For the sake of the transcript, I'd like to say that the Prosecution provided us with this document pursuant to Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question about local law. This statement was filed on the 15th of December, 1993. The witness was 16 years at the time. Can minors be interviewed without having someone accompanying them?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, the witness could have been interviewed without his parents being present, but I'm not sure who else was present during his interview since we have certain parts that have been deleted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the penal code of Bosnia-Herzegovina is this provided for?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say what the laws in force were on the 15th of December, 1993, because at the time there were laws in force which concerned the military period, the wartime period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll verify this. In the English translation I don't have the translation of the body responsible for the statement. Could you read it out in B/C/S. I can see that this took place in Bugojno. It must have been the Ministry of the Interior. Can you read out the title of the body concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. This is an official translation that we have received from the Prosecution. It says at the top of the document "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre Zenica, sector SDB-RO SDB Bugojno." SDB is the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, but could we go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two or three small questions and then my client will also have a couple of technical questions, so we'll be through quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. On behalf of General Praljak I will ask you a few questions to clear up some minor points. First of all, tell me, please, you explained to Their Honours today something that you didn't tell the investigators, that even though the whole village is called Zdrimci, you local people distinguish several parts of the village known as Perici, Trkici, Polici, and Sekerija. Can you please explain, can these parts of the village be called hamlets?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, because where the Perici live the area is known as Perici by the surname of that family. The same applies to Polici, after the surname Polic. Trkic and Sekerija, these are all surnames, and that is how the localities came to be known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you make this distinction yourselves, or is there a clear distinction made by the municipal authorities? Because on a map I note that Perici do exist, but on the other hand, I didn't find Sekerija, Polici, and Trkici. In these hamlets, is there a board saying "Polici", a signpost?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't exist. I know this everyone else who lived there. The local inhabitants knew these places by those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, from what you have just told us, can we conclude that you local people know exactly which part of Zdrimci is called the names that you gave us? You local villagers know this; is that right? Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I really did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My mistake. I probably didn't put it clearly. From what you have just said, is it right to say that the people of Zdrimci know exactly that this part of the village is called such-and-such and another part such-and-such?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me just one more thing. In this connection these parts of the village, Polici, Trkici, Sekerija, are they recognisable or, rather, separated physically? Is it visible that they're separate within this whole?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. We -- we never were separated. We all got on together fine. These parts were known after the surnames of the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I didn't put my question properly. Those parts, are they physically separate? Are they divided by a road or a vale or a hill? If I were to come as a stranger to the village, would I see that those are separate parts of the village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, you wouldn't. No, you wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, you described that in the house of Munib Trkic the women were in the basement and the men were upstairs on the ground floor. That is what you said in your statement. However, there's a difference in the numbers. How many of you were there in the -- on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
