utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, I said a moment ago, but between 7 and 10 men. But I'm not sure of the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I were to remind you that in your statement to the investigators on the 14th of January, 2004, you said some 15; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know exactly how many. There may not have been 15 or so. I just don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did all those who were present there have weapons or only some?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. Only three or four rifles were there. The others didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned the rifle M-48.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: M-48 is a military weapon, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some hunting rifles, maybe two, maybe even three. As I was saying a moment ago, my father brought a 48, but as far as I remember the others were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any Kalashnikovs there?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you surrendered, you said that you were taken to other houses where people were also surrendering from the basements. Is it true that in those houses, on the ground floor or in the vicinity of those houses, there were armed local men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Wherever there were men, where there were five or six men together, maybe again they had three or four rifles, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view the fact that you told us that there were a total of 35 of you in the garage, you said they were mostly men of military age, except you, and you said several older men. This number of about 35, of course you can't know exactly, those are the men who were defending those houses?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. But the others, I don't think all of them had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were captured, when you had surrendered, and when you were rounded up before being taken to the garage, is it true that the first questions put to you by HVO soldiers was about the weapons or, rather, they required you to surrender your weapons? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted these weapons to be handed over, but most of them had already been surrendered and disarmed, but they would say who hadn't surrendered their weapons on who had what kind of weapon. That was what they asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they first took your weapons as soon as you left the house? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then again when you were all gathered in one spot they again checked whether anyone had any weapons left and whether they had all surrendered their weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain why the HVO sent you from the garage to Vrse? What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you what task I was given. They just told me to tell them how we had fared so that they, too, should surrender. I really don't know what task they gave me. They just told me to go and tell them to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, that was the task, to go and tell them to surrender, but whom, to whom?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Probably to the people in Vrse. Probably when the attacks took place whoever was up there, members of the BH army. I was to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in Vrse there was a unit of the BH army there?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is a Muslim village, and those were local people. It is a larger village than Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you said it was about a kilometre and a half from your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for the elevation, is the village of Vrse a bit higher in relation to Zdrimci?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a bit higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you can see a good part of Zdrimci from the village of Vrse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you can see a good part of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Baba hill when they fired at your village, could it also be fired at from Vrse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's the other side. So it couldn't be fired at from there. I saw fire being opened from Baba because it's on the other side. So you can see the shooting. It's the other side in relation to Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure you understood the question quite well, the question of His Honour. Trkic's house that you were in, you saw from that house that they were opening fire from Baba, but other parts of the village, other Muslim parts, were being shot at from Vrse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. When they were firing from Baba, then they fired at the whole village. I personally didn't see any shots being fired from Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there fire opened on the Croatian part of the village from Vrse at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I wish to specify and avoid all ambiguity. We have just discovered that the BiH troops were in Vrse. Let us imagine that the HVO is on the Baba hill. Could they shoot from there at the BiH forces and at your village at the same time? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. As far as I can remember, HVO soldiers were up on Baba. As for the village of Vrse, there were the locals there, the inhabitants. Now, I don't know what they had, but I actually saw fire coming from Baba where the HVO soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question is more specific than that. Let us assume that from Baba the HVO is opening fire on Vrse because there's the BiH there. Could a shell fall on your village as a result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be possible, but a shell can't fall where I was. It could fall on a different part of the village, should that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Tell me, Witness, before this event in your village in January, 1993, would your father go to the front lines against the Serbs for shifts?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was in Austria, and I came just before the conflict started, so I don't know whether he went there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you can't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to clear up this question of the Baba hill. We're going to show you on the ELMO a map that General Praljak has provided for us, and I want you to have a look on the map, find the village of Vrse, and show us the Baba hill on that map. In that way, we will see straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. There's a good map. It might be helpful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This map is excellent, so we'll stick to it. Very well. Will you please mark with the pen or your finger, point to your village on the map. Show us your village on the map, please. It's more to the right. Further right, further right. There you are. You see? Here's your village. And there's Vrse which is higher up. Now, the Baba hill, where is the Baba hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you point the pen on the hill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Baba hill. I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the village, and this is Vrse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Baba, with your pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only rising keeping with a direction that Your Honour gave last week about follow-up questions arising from questions that the Bench may put, and it may be more appropriate to ask the short question now that I have. I wondered if it's prudent to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: I wondered if it's prudent to ask the witness what the distance between the Baba hill and the village of Vrse is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To the best of your recollection, how many kilometres between Baba and Vrse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe two kilometres, but again I must say that I don't know exactly. Maybe about two kilometres. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this can easily be found out by measuring the map because we know the scale. I have done with my cross-examination, if Mr. Praljak may be allowed to address a couple of questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Muamer, I'll ask you some very simple questions. Do you know whether before the 18th of January, 1993, there were any battles on Baba itself? Did you hear the sound of shooting at Baba? Baba is quite long. There's one end towards Karamustafic and the other towards your village. Was there any fighting before that at Baba?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know there weren't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether at Baba, towards the Karamustafic part, did anyone from your village dig any trenches in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Never mind. If you don't know, you don't know. When you went to the village of Vrse before and after these events, did you see trenches dug by the BH army around the village? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the second conflict, when the second conflict started between the HVO and the army, I did see those trenches turned towards Baba.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you mention the second conflict, are you referring to the one in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it started, but after the truce, when I was already at Vrse, then the second conflict started, and then I saw that there were some trenches there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But before the 18th of January, January, 1993, do you know -- because you can see that with your own eyes, do you know that the BH army had dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they weren't there. There weren't any trenches there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And when you went to Vrse you saw those trenches or not?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. I saw them in the second conflict, that the trenches were dug when the second conflict started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, did you join the regular army of Bosnia and Herzegovina later on? Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you can't know that a mortar shell is an anti-infantry weapon. It can't destroy a house, it can only damage it.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I know that it can destroy a house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That it can or it cannot?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can destroy a part of the house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I see, a part. Do you know were the villages in your -- were the houses in your village mixed?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: In the area I lived in only Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in the other part they were they mixed?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did shells fall on both parts when they fell?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know they fell in my part of the village. That's what I saw. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be able to follow what General Praljak is saying, you said that there were anti-aircraft guns also. Did you see this or did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from the people around me, from -- and I saw where the fire was coming from when a mortar is fired, and I also saw the anti-aircraft guns. I heard from them that they were this kind of artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you ever see the firing of a mortar shell? Can you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't nearby but I saw the fire, and I heard from them that it was being fired from this kind of artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: An anti-aircraft gun has a 20-millimetre bullet. Did you see one with two or three barrels?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I never saw them from close up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us all the ugly things that happened to you. So they beat people, you said, and then they buried some people alive, and then they forced them to do Christian prayers, and they torched houses. Now, listen to me carefully. Did you in any single case see a group of soldiers or was it only one or two, or was it always a group of soldiers? And if it was a group, did you ever see a commander with them giving them an order?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. I would see groups of men, but I never saw a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the events that you have listed, was it always an individual or maybe two people making such demands or was it a unit with a commander?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, not with a commander. It would be a small group. Some came from outside the village, and this other one was telling them what to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And this person was from your village, your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. If you're referring to Marko Vukadin, that wasn't him. These were strangers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many strangers were there when they required the women to say prayers?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I saw a man showing them how to cross themselves, and then to the side there were some more soldiers. I don't know exactly how many, but quite a number of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could a 1991 population census be put on the ELMO, though it was not adopted in the Assembly, from which we see that there were 759 Muslims in Zdrimci and 362 Croats. 759 Muslims -- I'm sorry, 759 Croats and 362 Muslims. Now, listen to me. Out of 362 Muslims, half are women, half men. If we don't count the elderly and children, we would have about 140 able-bodied men left. Since the HVO captured 30 to 40 soldiers, where were the other men from the village? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: The other men, before the shooting started that morning, a group had left the village. I really don't know how many men. There may have been about 20 men who had left the village. They may have even gone to Vrse. I don't know where they went. But the other men, when you're asking me about this number, many men were abroad, working in the West.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: How many were working in the West, because there are about 120 men missing. If the conflict in Gornji Vakuf started much earlier than the 18th of January, how did these people know that there was some sort of a conflict or HVO attack, as you call it, would start on the 18th of January? How did they know? Were they tapping the communications and then left the village? Where were the other men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Probably they knew, or they had a feeling about it. I don't know how they knew. They probably felt that this was coming and they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already asked you the same question at the beginning of the afternoon because I wanted to know whether there was a group of individuals who left, and you didn't give me a precise answer. Now you're just telling us that there was a group of 20 to 30 men who left the village to go to Vrse. And these men who left the village, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I remember well, but I mentioned earlier on in my statement that some people had left the night before. They had left the village. Now, whether they were all armed or not, I don't know. Some were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I wonder if I am good enough in arithmetics, but I would like to ask a question about the numbers used by General Praljak and it is about the numbers when you mentioned that there were roughly 360 Muslims in the village and, of course, again roughly -- then it should have been 180 men. And out of 180, you said that if we leave out, let's say, elderly and children, then we may have 140 able-bodied men. I'm not quite sure of this figure, because, anyway, if you take children, I mean, boys, and if you take also the elderly, then probably it is -- it would be more than -- altogether more than 40 which now subtracted from the 180. But of course I don't want to concentrate on the numbers, but in my view the number of those Muslims who had -- I mean Muslim men who could have been taken into account in my own counting shouldn't be more than, let's say, around 100. So I wanted to make this -- to mention these figures to show that we cannot have a kind of, a very increased number of men when we speak about the Muslim persons who might have been able bodied and, as such, could have been fought there at that village or outside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. This question seemed to be addressed to you. According to your calculations, well, how can you draw the conclusion that there were a hundred military-able Muslim men since the witness has said that some of these men had gone to work abroad? So how is it that you reached a figure of a hundred men who were military-able men?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military-able men are men between the age of 18 and 65 according to the law that was in force at the time. According to the average death rate, perhaps there was a margin of error of 5 to 6 per cent according to my calculations. If there are 181 men, we take away the women and those who were over 65 years of age. And the death rate, men die around the age of 80, well, if we take all these factors into consideration, I think my margin of error is not too bad. Even if we say that there were 130 or 125 military-able men, well, my question still stands. What happened to these 120 men? And even if we take away the men who were abroad, there were refugees from Jajce, from Donji Vakuf, et cetera. So I think my calculations are not too far off the mark, and the margin of error shouldn't be more than 5 or 6 per cent. But I have received an answer, and that's all I can ask for, so I thank you and I would like to thank the witness too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time to have the break. We'll resume at five to 6.00, and we should conclude by 7.00 p.m., after the other Defence teams have completed their examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I'm representing General Milivoj Petkovic, and I have a few simple questions for you. I would just like to clarify some of your testimony. Have a look at the Prosecution document that you have before you, P 01636. Could we see this document on the screen once more, please. If I've made a good note of what you've said, Mr. Trkic, you said that individuals under numbers 24 and 25 in the document were with you in the garage in your village. Is that correct? Do you remember that? It's on page 1 of the document. It says "List of prisoners who were released from Prozor prison." You mentioned the individuals who were with you in the garage and who were later taken to Prozor. Do you remember the individuals listed under numbers 24 and 25 here?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You do. They were with you in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Raif Curic from Bugojno and Dzemal Causevic from Gornji Vakuf; is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: I really didn't hear the names you mentioned now. 24, Mirsad Trkic, and 25, Enver Trkic. I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the first page of the document. Do you have the first page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who is listed under number 24 and number 25?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the wrong document on the screen, on e-court. I'm not asking the witness anything about this list right now. Could we have list A, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trkic, can you see that now?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The text to the left is in English, but you can recognise the names in spite of that fact. Do you know the individuals listed under numbers 24 and 25?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you say that they were with you in the garage?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No. I apologise. I don't know number 24, Raif Curic. I don't know this person. But I also don't know Dzemal Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So these persons were not in the garage with you. Very well. We clarified that matter, because I wanted to know how those persons got to Strimac [as interpreted]. You said the shooting commenced on the 18th of January at 6.00 in the morning, and on that occasion the women were in the basement and the men in the business premises above the office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you spend the night in the basement or, rather, on the floor above the basement?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't spend the night there because we were taken to the garage that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the previous night, the night before the shooting started. Did you spend that night in the house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't spend the entire night there. We were there, but we went home and stayed there for a while and then we returned. So we were there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you explain this? At night you would return home, and then you'd come back to the house that you were staying in.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to my house in the course of the night, and my mother and sister did so too. We returned to my house up until about 10.00 or 12.00 at night, and then when we returned to the house, that's where we were when the shooting broke out in the morning, and we didn't leave the house any more. We were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell me, did you spend the other days and previous nights in a similar way in that house? Did you spend some time in the house and also leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We spent most of our time in our houses. But as one felt the situation changing, well, one acted on that basis, but we were mostly in our houses. And then we'd go to this other house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you be precise? When did you start gathering in these four houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be precise. I know about the house or, rather, the house that my mother and I were in. Three or four nights later on, well, we'd go to the basement and then we'd return home. The shooting wasn't very intensive at the time, so we weren't there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you spent three or four nights like that. Who decided in the village that the population would take shelter in this manner, would take shelter in these houses that had been selected as shelters?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the other houses. I know about the situation in the case of my house, because my mother and father wanted to go to the basement. They probably realised something was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you overhear any conversations about an attack being expected, about it being necessary to prepare to defend the village?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything of that kind. We just went up there because my parents wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. After you'd been released from the garage, you said that a while later you went to live with your sister in the village of Vrse. Now, I quote you: You said it was because you didn't want to stay on in your house because you didn't know whether a conflict would break out. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went to my sister's. We all went to live there because we weren't sure that a conflict wouldn't break out again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you had decided to remain in your village, in your house, could you have done so? There were no objective reasons preventing you from acting in this way?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if I had so decided, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you have, in fact, stayed on in your village and lived in your house? Was it possible to live in that house?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't possible since the shooting had broken out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Had the house been burnt down or not? That's the sense of my question. When I ask you whether you could have lived in it had you wanted to, that's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, part of it caught fire but it hadn't burnt down entirely. So perhaps it would have been possible to live in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words, the house was in such a condition that it would have been possible to live in it if you had wanted do so?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that about 10 HVO soldiers entered the village, and they were escorting a man who was heading towards the house you were in, and you mentioned the term "human shield." What does the term -- or what does the expression "human shield" mean in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the conclusion I drew because the soldiers were walking behind the man and the man was in front of them. He didn't have any weapons and they were spurring him on. They were following him, so that's how I put it, but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that the conclusion that you drew or did you hear this from other villagers? Did other villagers use this expression?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's how it looked like to me and that's what I said. That's how I put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So now that you think about this expression again, if you imagine a person walking in front of 10 men, well, can such a person be a shield for those men?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: Well, no, but if the men behind him are armed and their rifles are at the ready and if he doesn't have a rifle, well, that's how things appeared to me, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When the HVO soldiers entered the village, did anyone open fire from any of the houses, any of the houses that the HVO soldiers were approaching?

utterances.speaker: MUAMER TRKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no, there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Next Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have another Defence team. Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Prosecution have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, no thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, this completes your testimony. On behalf of the Judges, I would like to thank you for having come here and having contributed to establishing the truth. I wish you a safe trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and the Victims and Witnesses Unit will then take care of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as far as tomorrow's schedule is concerned, we'll be hearing a witness over a three-day period, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness for the rest of the week essentially will be the one starting tomorrow. So we are on schedule, and that's the programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as I can remember, the Prosecution had planned on having four hours for the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's right, Your Honour. It was something that we thought would be reasonably doable, including cross-examination, for the rest of the week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have a little time at our disposal. Are there any issues that anyone would like to raise? Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes. Just one matter very briefly. We have to file tomorrow two responses to Prosecution motions for the admission of evidence under Rule 92 bis. Your Honour, in both of those cases the motions filed by the Prosecution exceeded the word limit by a slight amount, not very much at all, and I think Mr. Scott and I take the same position on that, that it's not our way to really object to those things, but in the same vein we would like permission to exceed the word limit by no more than 1 or 200 words in each case in order to fully respond to the motion, and I would make a oral application. I don't think there was an application by the Prosecution, but of course we would have no objection whatsoever and we don't take any point on that. So I would ask the Court to authorise us to slightly exceed the word limit on both of those responses that will be filed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll grant your request and you may have 200 words, up to 200 words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any other issues to be raised? No. Tomorrow we will resume with our hearings, and as you're well aware, we will commence at 2.15. I wish you a good evening.
